seasons.title: Japan
seasons.tagline: Word puzzles from Sapporo to Okinawa.

stops.fact: Bonsai are ordinary trees, kept small by pruning and wiring. Some in Japan are over 500 years old and have outlived a dozen owners.

stops.hint: Where you clap twice at the gate
stops.fact: Shinto shrines are marked by a torii gate. Visitors bow, clap twice, and bow again to greet the kami who lives there.

stops.hint: Bells, incense and a giant bronze Buddha
stops.fact: Todai-ji in Nara holds a bronze Buddha 15 metres tall. The wooden hall around it was once the largest wooden building on Earth.

stops.hint: An artist of dance, song and conversation
stops.fact: Geisha means "art person". Apprentices in Kyoto are called maiko and train for years in dance, music and the tea ceremony.
In Japan, slurping ramen or soba loudly is polite. It cools the noodles and tells the cook you are enjoying them.

stops.hint: Raked gravel and one perfect stone
stops.fact: Ryoan-ji's rock garden has 15 stones. From any seat on the veranda, one is always hidden from view.

stops.hint: Japan has more than 14,000 of them
stops.fact: Japan counts over 14,000 islands. Only about 430 are inhabited, and four make up nearly all the land.
Japanese pagodas have a central pillar that hangs loose. It lets the tower sway in earthquakes, and almost none have ever fallen.
Chochin paper lanterns still hang outside izakaya bars. A red one means the kitchen is open and the sake is cold.
Karate means "empty hand". It grew in Okinawa, where weapons were banned, and joined the Olympics in Tokyo in 2021.

stops.hint: Two swords and a code of honour
stops.fact: Samurai wore two swords: the long katana and the short wakizashi. Wearing both was a right no commoner had.
Kyoto's Kennin-ji has twin dragons painted across its ceiling. Legend says a dragon painted with eyes will fly away.

stops.hint: Japan has over 100 that still breathe
stops.fact: Japan has about 110 active volcanoes, a tenth of the world's total. Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707.

stops.hint: Where the black ships came in
stops.fact: Commodore Perry's black ships sailed into Edo Bay in 1853. Within 15 years the shogunate had fallen.
Japan's imperial line is the oldest continuous monarchy in the world. Emperor Naruhito is counted as the 126th.
For nearly 700 years the shogun ran Japan while the emperor stayed in Kyoto. The last one stepped down in 1867.
Matcha is whole tea leaves ground to powder. One bowl holds the caffeine of a coffee and the ritual of a ceremony.
True origami uses one square sheet with no cuts or glue. A thousand paper cranes is a wish for recovery.

stops.hint: Batter that came with the Portuguese
stops.fact: Tempura arrived with Portuguese missionaries in the 1500s. The name likely comes from the Latin for the fasting seasons.
Karaoke means "empty orchestra". The first machine was built in Kobe in 1971 by a musician who never patented it.
Tsunami is Japanese for "harbour wave". The word entered English after the 1896 Sanriku wave.
Japan sees about 25 typhoons a year. The 1281 typhoon that wrecked a Mongol fleet gave the world the word kamikaze.

stops.hint: The one who was born before
stops.fact: Sensei literally means "one born earlier". It is used for teachers, doctors, lawyers and manga artists alike.
Sashimi is raw fish without rice. At Tokyo's Toyosu market a single bluefin tuna has sold for over two million dollars.

stops.hint: An old word for the emperor
stops.fact: Mikado was a poetic name for the emperor. It also named the pick-up-sticks game and a famous comic opera.
Sapporo's Snow Festival builds ice sculptures the size of buildings every February. The beer has brewed here since 1876.
Okinawa has one of the highest shares of people over 100 in the world. Its secret is said to be sweet potato and purpose.
Daimyo were regional lords under the shogun. They had to spend every other year in Edo, which kept them loyal and broke.
Shinto is Japan's native faith with no founder and no scripture. Eight million kami live in mountains, trees and rivers.
Ikebana is the art of flower arranging. Empty space matters as much as the stems, and each arrangement suggests a season.

stops.hint: A heated table with a blanket
stops.fact: A kotatsu is a low table with a heater under it and a quilt over it. Winter in Japan is spent with your legs inside one.
Narita airport opened in 1978 after years of farmer protests. One holdout farm still sits inside the airport grounds.
Up to 3,000 people cross Shibuya's scramble at every green light. Hachikō the loyal dog waited outside the station here for nine years.

stops.hint: An inn with futons and a bath
stops.fact: A ryokan is a traditional inn: tatami floors, a futon laid out at night and a hot bath. One in Yamanashi has taken guests since the year 705.

stops.hint: The fox that guards the shrine
stops.fact: Kitsune, the fox, is the messenger of Inari. Thousands of fox statues guard Inari shrines, many with the key to the rice store in their mouths.

stops.hint: The raccoon dog by the shop door
stops.fact: Tanuki statues stand outside shops and restaurants with a straw hat, a sake flask and a big belly, promising good luck and good business.

journey.title: Mexico
journey.tagline: From the cenotes to the capital.

stops.hint: Corn dough steamed in a husk
stops.fact: Find the baby figure in your slice of Three Kings cake on 6 January and you owe everyone tamales on 2 February.
A classic piñata star has seven points, one for each deadly sin. Breaking it blindfolded stood for faith beating temptation.

stops.hint: They built their city on a lake
stops.fact: The Aztecs founded their capital where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a snake. That scene is on Mexico's flag today.

stops.hint: Named after the man who made them
stops.fact: Nachos were born in 1943 in Piedras Negras, when Ignacio "Nacho" Anaya fried tortilla chips with cheese for guests who came after closing.

stops.hint: Jungle sinkholes full of blue water
stops.fact: Yucatán's cenotes form a ring around the buried crater of the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. The Maya saw them as doors to the underworld.
Mexico's biggest fiesta starts on the night of 15 September, when the president rings the bell Hidalgo rang in 1810 and leads the Grito.
Monarchs fly about 4,000 km from Canada to Mexico's fir forests. They arrive for Day of the Dead, and many call them returning souls.

stops.hint: A shadow slides down the steps
stops.fact: At each equinox the late sun at Chichén Itzá casts a shadow snake down the pyramid's steps, joining a stone serpent head at the base.

stops.hint: The salamander that never grows up
stops.fact: Axolotls live wild only in the canals of Xochimilco. One can regrow a lost leg, and even parts of its heart and brain.

stops.hint: Blue agave in a shot glass
stops.fact: Tequila can only be made from blue agave in five Mexican states, mostly Jalisco. Each plant grows for years before its heart is roasted.
Mexico mines more silver than any other country. Its silver dollars were so trusted they were legal money in the United States until 1857.

stops.hint: A rainbow beak in the jungle
stops.fact: A toucan's huge bill is light and full of blood vessels. It works like a radiator, letting the bird shed heat in the forests of southern Mexico.
Mexico has more Spanish speakers than any other country, over twice as many as Spain. It also recognises 68 Indigenous languages.
Mexico has more kinds of cactus than any other country, most found nowhere else. Prickly pear pads, nopales, are eaten as a vegetable.

stops.hint: How a luchador hides his face
stops.fact: In lucha libre a mask is sacred and lost only in a bet match. The legend El Santo was buried in his silver mask in 1984.

stops.hint: An orchid that flavours ice cream
stops.fact: Vanilla is a Mexican orchid that would not fruit abroad without its native bees, until a boy of 12 on Réunion learned to hand-pollinate it in 1841.
Around 500 BC the Zapotecs levelled a mountaintop in Oaxaca to build Monte Albán. Benito Juárez, Mexico's great president, was Zapotec.

stops.hint: Six strings in a mariachi band
stops.fact: Mariachi grew up in Jalisco. A band mixes violins, trumpets and several kinds of guitar, and UNESCO named it world heritage in 2011.
The Yucatán peninsula has almost no rivers on the surface. Rain sinks through the limestone into the longest flooded caves ever mapped.

stops.hint: Lit to guide the dead home
stops.fact: For Day of the Dead, families light candles and lay paths of orange marigold petals so the souls of loved ones can find their way home.
Burrito means "little donkey". It comes from northern Mexico, where wheat grows well and flour tortillas are an everyday food.

stops.hint: Canyons the colour of a penny
stops.fact: Copper Canyon is six canyons in one, far bigger than the Grand Canyon. Its Rarámuri people are famous for running huge distances in sandals.

stops.hint: Frida painted on one in bed
stops.fact: After a bus crash in 1925, Frida Kahlo painted in bed on a special easel, with a mirror overhead. So her first subject was herself.
Divers at La Quebrada in Acapulco have leapt 35 metres into a narrow cove since 1934, timing each dive to land as a wave rolls in.

stops.hint: Hot pods first grown in Mexico
stops.fact: Chili peppers were first farmed in Mexico about 6,000 years ago. The word chili comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.

stops.hint: They fly from the top of a pole
stops.fact: The Voladores of Papantla spin down a tall pole on ropes, four flyers, 13 turns each. That makes 52, the years of one sacred calendar cycle.
Tula's stone warriors stand over 4.5 metres tall. The Aztecs admired the Toltecs so much that their name came to mean master craftsman.

stops.hint: Where the morning loaves come from
stops.fact: In France, only a shop that kneads and bakes its own bread on site may call itself a boulangerie. The baguette joined UNESCO's list in 2022.
The Louvre began as a fortress around 1190 and later became a royal palace. Its medieval moat walls still stand in the basement.

stops.hint: A grand house in the Loire
stops.fact: Chambord's double staircase lets two people climb at the same time without ever meeting. Leonardo da Vinci may have sketched the idea.

stops.hint: Choux pastry with a shiny glaze
stops.fact: Éclair is French for lightning, perhaps because one is eaten in a flash. The same choux dough makes profiteroles and cream puffs.
Chamonix, at the foot of Mont Blanc, hosted the very first Winter Olympics in 1924. Mont Blanc itself was first climbed in 1786.

stops.hint: Feathers, cancan and a red windmill
stops.fact: The Moulin Rouge opened in 1889, the same year as the Eiffel Tower. Toulouse-Lautrec painted its cancan dancers and made them famous.

stops.hint: A gift that crossed the Atlantic
stops.fact: The Statue of Liberty was France's gift to the United States in 1886. Its iron skeleton was designed by Gustave Eiffel, three years before his tower.

stops.hint: Two almond shells and a filling
stops.fact: Long before Paris made them pastel, macarons were plain almond cookies. Saint-Émilion still bakes them to a nuns' recipe said to date from 1620.

stops.hint: The azure coast of the south
stops.fact: Nice's seafront is the Promenade des Anglais, named for the English who spent their winters there. The name Côte d'Azur dates from 1887.
A critic mocked Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise in 1874, and the insult stuck: the whole movement became Impressionism.
The metre was born in revolutionary France: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured through Paris.

stops.hint: Slurped raw with a squeeze of lemon
stops.fact: France grows more oysters than the rest of the EU put together. Louis XIV had them sent fresh to Versailles from Cancale, near Saint-Malo.

stops.hint: Walls within walls on a hilltop
stops.fact: Carcassonne has two rings of walls, 3 km long, and 52 towers. Their pointed slate roofs were added in the 1800s, and people still argue about them.
Grasse in Provence is called the perfume capital of the world. Its jasmine is still picked by hand in the early morning, when the scent is strongest.
In 1988 three steps led down to the ice cave in the Mer de Glace, France's longest glacier. It has melted so much that it now takes hundreds.
A Montmartre plaque says Russian soldiers in 1814 shouted "bystro", quickly, and named the bistro. Linguists say the word came decades later.

stops.hint: The bird on the team shirt
stops.fact: Notre-Dame's copper rooster fell with the spire in the 2019 fire and was found dented in the rubble. Its 2023 successor has wings of flame.
On 28 December 1895 the Lumière brothers showed ten short films to a paying crowd in a Paris café. The movies were born that night.
Dijon mustard is made with white wine or verjuice instead of vinegar. About four in five of the seeds France uses are grown in Canada.

stops.hint: Six raised dots, read by touch
stops.fact: Louis Braille lost his sight at 3 and invented his dot alphabet at 15. He lies in the Panthéon, but his home village kept his hands.
In 1858 a girl named Bernadette saw visions in a grotto here. Lourdes now has more hotels than any French city except Paris.
Haute couture is a protected name in France that only approved houses may use. Coco Chanel opened her first couture house in Biarritz in 1915.
"Let them eat cake" was really "let them eat brioche", and Marie Antoinette never said it. Rousseau wrote it when she was a child in Austria.

stops.hint: The pack in the Tour de France
stops.fact: The Tour de France leader wears yellow because L'Auto, the newspaper that started the race in 1903, was printed on yellow paper.

stops.hint: The year on the wine label
stops.fact: A wine's vintage is the year its grapes were picked. Most champagne blends several years; a vintage champagne is made only in great ones.
In 1885 Pasteur saved a boy of nine, bitten by a rabid dog, with the first rabies vaccine. The boy grew up to be the Pasteur Institute's caretaker.

stops.hint: The city a teenage girl set free
stops.fact: In 1429 Joan of Arc, aged about 17, broke the English siege of Orléans in nine days, then led the king to be crowned at Reims.
Gelato has less fat than ice cream and is churned slowly, so it holds less air. It is served warmer, which makes the flavour stronger.

stops.hint: The city where streets are water
stops.fact: Venice rests on millions of wooden piles driven into the lagoon mud. Kept away from the air, the wood has held the city up for centuries.

stops.hint: He came, he saw, he conquered
stops.fact: Julius Caesar was stabbed on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC. The month of July is still named after him.
Some olive trees in Puglia are over a thousand years old and still bear fruit. The region makes more olive oil than any other in Italy.
Pisa's tower began to tilt in 1178, five years into building, because of soft ground. The builders curved the upper floors to make up for it.
Milan's risotto is golden with saffron. Legend says a glassmaker working on the cathedral's windows added it to a wedding feast in 1574.

stops.hint: Rowed with one oar, standing up
stops.fact: A gondola is built lopsided, one side wider than the other, so a single oar keeps it going straight. Nearly every one is painted black.
Naples is the home of pizza. The Margherita is said to be named after Queen Margherita, its tomato, mozzarella and basil matching the flag.

stops.hint: The stone David was carved from
stops.fact: Michelangelo's David was cut from a block of Carrara marble that other sculptors had given up on. He was 26 when he started.
Vatican City is the world's smallest country. In 1527 its Swiss Guard held off an army while the pope fled to Castel Sant'Angelo.

stops.hint: Sniffed out by a dog in the woods
stops.fact: Italy banned pigs from truffle hunting in 1985: they dig up the ground and eat the prize. A big white truffle has sold for over $100,000.
The Vespa was launched in 1946 to get Italy moving after the war. Its name means "wasp", for its buzzing engine and narrow waist.

stops.hint: Dark green spires on Tuscan hills
stops.fact: Val d'Orcia's cypress hills were shaped by Siena's merchants in the 1300s and 1400s as an ideal landscape. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

stops.hint: All roads led to its capital
stops.fact: The Roman Empire's greatest arena, the Colosseum, opened in 80 AD with 100 days of games. It could seat around 50,000 people.
Amalfi's lemons grow on steep terraces under frames of chestnut poles. Their peel, steeped in alcohol and sweetened, becomes limoncello.
Antonio Vivaldi was a Venetian priest nicknamed "the Red Priest" for his hair. He wrote much of his music for an orphanage's all-girl orchestra.
Castel del Monte in Puglia is an octagon with eight octagonal towers. It is the building on Italy's 1 cent euro coin.

stops.hint: Red wine with a black rooster
stops.fact: The black rooster on Chianti Classico recalls a legend: Florence starved its rooster, so it crowed first and won a border race with Siena.
Fresco paint goes onto wet plaster and becomes part of the wall. Michelangelo painted the Sistine ceiling this way, standing, not lying down.

stops.hint: Steps of vines above the sea
stops.fact: Cinque Terre's vineyards climb terraces held up by dry-stone walls with no mortar. End to end, the walls would run for thousands of kilometres.
In northern Italy, hot polenta is poured onto a wooden board in the middle of the table and cut with a string, not a knife.
Juliet's balcony in Verona was added to a medieval house in the 1930s. Volunteers still answer thousands of letters sent to Juliet every year.

stops.hint: The man who saw Jupiter's moons
stops.fact: Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564. A finger taken from his body in 1737 is on show in a Florence museum, pointing at the sky.

stops.hint: Pulls your espresso at the bar
stops.fact: In Italy, coffee is cheaper standing at the bar than sitting at a table. Ask for "un caffe" and you get an espresso.
Dante wrote the Inferno after Florence exiled him in 1302. In 2008 the city voted to lift his sentence, nearly 700 years late.
Stromboli has erupted almost nonstop for over 2,000 years. Sailors call its glowing summit the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.
Palermo was founded by the Phoenicians and later ruled by Arabs and Normans. Its arancine rice balls are named after little oranges.

journey.title: Egypt
journey.tagline: Up the Nile, past the pyramids.

stops.fact: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years, until Lincoln Cathedral's spire passed it around 1311.
Donkeys, not camels, hauled supplies for the pyramid builders. Camels only became common in Egypt over 1,500 years later.
Napoleon's soldiers did not shoot off the Sphinx's nose. Drawings made decades before they arrived already show it missing.
In Egypt it is called ta'ameya and made from fava beans, not chickpeas, with so many herbs that it is bright green inside.
Cairo's Khan el-Khalili has been trading since the 1380s. Its Fishawy cafe has poured tea in the same alley for over 200 years.

stops.hint: The king who was a living god
stops.fact: Pharaoh comes from per-aa, "great house", the royal palace. Like "the White House", the building's name came to mean the ruler.

stops.hint: Where the call to prayer rings
stops.fact: Cairo is nicknamed the city of a thousand minarets. Al-Azhar mosque, founded in 970, is also one of the oldest universities in the world.

stops.hint: Mo Salah's game, by its US name
stops.fact: Egypt has won the Africa Cup of Nations seven times, more than any other country. The national team is nicknamed the Pharaohs.
In 2021, 22 royal mummies rode across Cairo in golden cars to a new museum, a night procession called the Pharaohs' Golden Parade.
Koshary piles rice, lentils, macaroni and chickpeas under spicy tomato sauce and crispy fried onions. It is often called Egypt's national dish.

stops.hint: The Wonder that lit the harbour
stops.fact: Alexandria's Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders. Qaitbay's fort now stands on its site, and French still calls a lighthouse a phare.
Pyramid builders were paid in rations of bread and barley beer. Egyptians still call bread aish, from the Arabic word for life.

stops.hint: A gift that went to Paris
stops.fact: One of Luxor Temple's twin obelisks has stood in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since 1836. Its partner still guards the temple gate.
At sunrise, dozens of hot-air balloons lift off over Luxor's west bank, drifting above temples, tombs and green fields by the Nile.
Our word paper comes from papyrus. Egyptians laid strips of the reed's pith crosswise and pressed them into sheets that last for millennia.

stops.hint: Two wheels, two horses, one king
stops.fact: Tutankhamun was buried with six chariots. They had to be taken apart to fit through the narrow passages of his tomb.
Horus, the falcon god, protected Egypt's kings. His temple at Edfu is one of the best preserved in Egypt, with granite falcons by its doors.
The Nile flows north while the wind mostly blows south. For thousands of years boats have sailed upstream and simply drifted back down.
Twice a year the sunrise reaches deep inside Abu Simbel to light statues of Ramses II and two gods. Ptah, a god of the underworld, stays in shadow.
Tunis, a village in Faiyum, had no potters until Swiss artist Evelyne Porret began teaching its children in the 1980s. Now it is famous for pottery.

stops.hint: A valley of them, in the sand
stops.fact: Wadi Al-Hitan holds fossil whales about 40 million years old. Some still have tiny hind legs, left over from ancestors that walked.
A desert mirage is not in your head. Hot air near the ground bends light from the sky so it looks like water, and a camera can photograph it.
By Bedouin custom a guest may stay three days before anyone asks why they came. In Sinai, Bedouin guides lead hikers through the canyons.

stops.hint: Mask, fins and a breathing tube
stops.fact: The Red Sea holds over 1,000 kinds of fish, and more than one in ten is found nowhere else on Earth.

stops.hint: Worth a 2 a.m. climb in Sinai
stops.fact: Hikers climb Mount Sinai at night to see dawn from its 2,285 m summit. A camel can carry you most of the way, but the last 750 steps are on foot.
Saint Catherine's Monastery is said to have the oldest library still in use. Only the Vatican holds more early manuscripts.

stops.hint: It spins in Red Sea lagoons
stops.fact: Spinner dolphins hunt at night and doze by day. A pod spends its days in the lagoon of Samadai Reef near Marsa Alam, nicknamed Dolphin House.
Namaste comes from Sanskrit and means "I bow to you". It works as hello and goodbye, to one person or a whole room.
India grows more mangoes than any other country, in over a thousand varieties. The prized Alphonso is named after a Portuguese general.
India is home to about three quarters of the world's wild tigers. The Ajanta Caves were found again in 1819 by a British officer out hunting one.
Jaipur's Hawa Mahal, the "Palace of Winds", has 953 little windows. Royal women watched the festivals in the street below without being seen.

stops.hint: A red ball and a billion fans
stops.fact: India won its first World Cup at Lord's in 1983. Ahmedabad's stadium holds about 132,000 fans, the biggest cricket ground on Earth.
Hyderabad and Lucknow each claim India's best biryani. Cooked dum style, the pot is sealed with dough so the rice steams in its own juices.
Cashmere wool is named after it. On Srinagar's Dal Lake, flower sellers paddle shikara boats from houseboat to houseboat.

stops.hint: Dances when the rain is coming
stops.fact: It is India's national bird. Its famous fan is not its tail but a train of long feathers growing above it, shed and regrown every year.

stops.hint: Wound by hand, every single day
stops.fact: Sikh men tie theirs fresh each day from several metres of cloth. At Amritsar's Golden Temple, every visitor covers their head.

stops.hint: Milk, oil and a hairy shell
stops.fact: In India one is cracked open to bless a fresh start, from a new car to a film's first day of shooting. Its husk is spun into coir rope.
It flows about 2,500 km from a Himalayan glacier to the Bay of Bengal. In Varanasi, lamps and bells greet it every evening.

stops.hint: The emperors who built the Taj
stops.fact: The Mughal emperors ruled much of India from 1526. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and Delhi's great Jama Masjid.
The festival of lights fills homes with little clay oil lamps called diyas, and doorsteps with rangoli patterns of coloured powder.

stops.hint: Teardrop swirls on a fine shawl
stops.fact: In India the teardrop swirl is often called ambi, after a mango. Europe met it on Kashmir shawls and named it after a Scottish weaving town.
It takes around 150,000 crocus flowers to make a kilo. Saffron is also the top band of the flag raised at the Red Fort every 15 August.

stops.hint: Trains past a sea of milk
stops.fact: Indian Railways employs over a million people. In Goa, its trains cross right in front of Dudhsagar, the "sea of milk" waterfall.

stops.hint: It once meant a head massage
stops.fact: The word comes from Hindi champo, "press". Sake Dean Mahomed took the massage to Brighton and became shampooing surgeon to King George IV.

stops.hint: Where Mowgli grew up with wolves
stops.fact: The word comes from Hindi jangal. Kipling set The Jungle Book in the Seoni hills of central India, near today's Pench Tiger Reserve.

stops.hint: A palace floats on its lake
stops.fact: Udaipur's Lake Palace seems to float on Lake Pichola. It starred in the 1983 James Bond film Octopussy.

stops.hint: The Koh-i-Noor is the famous one
stops.fact: Until the 1700s India was the world's only big source of diamonds. Visitors to Hampi in the 1500s saw them sold in its open street markets.

stops.hint: Clay oven, hot enough for naan
stops.fact: A tandoor can run hotter than 400 C. Naan is slapped onto its clay wall and bakes in a minute or two.

stops.hint: Loose trousers that went to bed
stops.fact: The word is Persian for "leg garment". British officers in India took them home in the 1800s, and they became nightwear.

stops.hint: Spotted cat at the city's edge
stops.fact: Mumbai is one of the few megacities with wild big cats inside its limits. Dozens of leopards live in Sanjay Gandhi National Park.

stops.hint: He walked to the sea for salt
stops.fact: In 1930 he walked about 390 km to the sea at Dandi to make salt, defying a British tax. His birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday.
Kerala's houseboats were once kettuvallam rice barges, built without a single nail and stitched together with coir rope.
Henna is painted on a bride's hands before the wedding. The groom's name is often hidden in the pattern for him to find.
Its old town is washed in blue below Mehrangarh Fort. Jodhpurs, the riding trousers, are named after it, thanks to its polo-playing princes.
